articles.title: CreatorMemBench v1.0: A Lifecycle Benchmark for Mutable Creator-Agent Memory
articles.abstract: CreatorMemBench v1.0 contains 20 synthetic creator timelines and 160 checkpoints for evaluating mutable long-term memory in creator agents. The benchmark covers stable identity, scoped preferences, multi-session composition, transient noise, updates, forgetting, retention, and resurrection. The archive includes separated inputs and gold criteria, a strict semantic scoring protocol, an offline aggregation script, a prediction schema, a license, and SHA-256 checksums. It contains no production conversations, account identifiers, credentials, proprietary service code, endpoint identifiers, or raw internal traces.

articles.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
articles.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.

articles.title: Data and code for: Who wins depends on who judges: re-grading published LoCoMo and LongMemEval answers of agent memory systems
articles.abstract: Verdicts, labels, tables and code for a study of how published long-term memory leaderboards for LLM agents depend on the LLM judge. The 47,253 unique answers that vendors and third parties published for 50 answer sets (36 LoCoMo, 14 LongMemEval-S; 10 memory products and 9 baselines) were re-graded by a grid of 20 judge configurations (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-5-mini on both benchmarks, gpt-4o on LongMemEval-S only, each with five prompts): 737,115 verdicts. A reference judge (gpt-5.4, reasoning effort low) graded 5,000 of the answers under the same five prompts: 25,000 verdicts. 250 disputed answers carry three-way labels (CORRECT, PARTIAL, WRONG) from an LLM annotator in two independent blind passes; these are model labels, not human labels. Question, gold and answer texts and raw judge replies are not included, because they belong to the benchmark authors and the vendors or can quote them. Every key resolves to the public source files listed with URL, commit and SHA-256 in code/manifest.json, and the included code rebuilds the aligned answers. See README.md.

articles.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
articles.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory, which creates a critical vulnerability that we study here: memory poisoning. An adversary can store untrusted content in one session that later steers a consequential action, such as a payment, a setting change, or data exfiltration, in a future session. Existing defenses base a memory item's authority to act on either its content (detection or trust-scoring) or its derivation history (lineage). We show that both signals are malleable. An attacker can launder an untrusted origin through three channels specific to LLM agents: the agent's own summarization, a trusted-tool echo, and manufactured corroboration. Each makes the content look benign and breaks or flips its derivation edge to ``trusted.'' We formalize malleability for the memory write-retrieve-act pipeline and prove a machine-checked separation theorem. No content- or lineage-based defense is sound under laundering (T1), write-time origin binding is necessary (T2), and non-malleable origin-bound authority with Sybil-resistant corroboration-gated elevation is sufficient (T3). Our construction, TMA-NM (Tamper-evident Memory Authority, Non-Malleable), instantiates non-malleable information-flow control (IFC) for LLM-agent memory. A cross-defense, cross-attack, and cross-model benchmark over eight frontier models shows that existing defenses fail exactly where the theory predicts (up to 68% laundering attack-success), while TMA-NM reaches 0% attack success on both direct and laundering attacks across all models and channels, at full legitimate utility. We release the benchmark, harness, and machine-checked TLA+ models to support reproducibility.

articles.title: MemMark: State-Evolution Attribution Watermarking for Agent Long-Term Memory Systems
articles.abstract: Memory-backed agents need provenance that can survive leaked or migrated snapshots, where logs, visible outputs, and trusted metadata may be absent. We propose MemMark, a state-evolution attribution watermark that embeds an owner-controlled signal into latent memory-write decisions. At each internal LLM call, MemMark samples among admissible candidates using keyed, distribution-preserving selection, and records cryptographic commitments with signed session anchors and reveal evidence. This makes attribution depend on reproducible backend behavior rather than mutable provenance fields. Across A-Mem and Graphiti on LoCoMo, with three LLM backbones, MemMark preserves memory utility: Overall F1 retains 99.6% of the unwatermarked baseline, while BLEU-1 changes by +0.2%. It also provides usable carrier capacity, with 1.16, 1.14, and 1.26 bits of mean entropy for update-target, link-target, and semantic-realization decisions. In the snapshot-only R3 setting, MemMark recovers the full 40-bit payload from final snapshots, while wrong-key verification remains near chance. Under nine memory-lifecycle attacks, verification distinguishes tampering, evidence deletion, and partial payload recovery. These results show that robust snapshot-only attribution is feasible for long-term agent memory without surviving traces, trusted metadata, or utility-degrading.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and anti-cancer drugs: advancing discovery, personalization, and precision oncology
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics. By summarizing current evidence and targeting research gaps, this review offers a clear view of how AI is enhancing the discovery, personalization, and validation of anticancer treatments.

articles.title: Explanation User Interfaces: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is one of the major technological advancements of this century, bearing incredible potential for users through AI-powered applications and tools in numerous domains. Being often black-box (i.e., its decision-making process is unintelligible), developers typically resort to eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to interpret the behavior of AI models to produce systems that are transparent, fair, reliable, and trustworthy. However, presenting explanations to the user is not trivial and is often left as a secondary aspect of the system’s design process, leading to AI systems that are not useful to end-users. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review on Explanation User Interfaces (XUIs) to gain a deeper understanding of the solutions and design guidelines employed in the academic literature to effectively present explanations to users. To improve the contribution and real-world impact of this survey, we also present a platform to support Human-cEnteRed developMent of Explainable user interfaceS (HERMES) and guide practitioners and scholars in the design and evaluation of XUIs.

articles.title: Case Report: Neonatal ultra-severe hemolytic anemia complicated by pulmonary hypertension induced by compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene and literature review
articles.abstract: Objective To investigate the clinical characteristics, genotypic profiles, and diagnostic/therapeutic strategies for congenital hemolytic anemia induced by compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene. Methods We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of a neonate who presented primarily with ultra-severe anemia, elevated direct bilirubin, and pulmonary hypertension. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was utilized for variant identification, followed by a comprehensive review of literature. Results The patient, a female neonate, developed severe anemia within 10 h of birth, accompanied by rapidly progressing hyperbilirubinemia (predominantly direct hyperbilirubinemia). Bedside echocardiography revealed a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary hypertension. Trio-WES identified pathogenic compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene: c.519_525dup (p.Gly176ArgfsTer179) and c.1012C > A (p.Pro338Thr). Following multiple red blood cell transfusions and mechanical ventilatory support, the infant's condition stabilized. During a 24-month follow-up, the patient exhibited transfusion-dependent anemia. Conclusion For neonates presenting with unexplained (Coombs/DAT-negative) severe hemolytic anemia, particularly when complicated by pulmonary hypertension and atypical cholestasis, early genetic testing should be performed to rule out KLF1 -related diseases.

articles.title: Identifying Harm in Personalized, Generative AI Systems Requires User-Centered Auditing at the Interaction Level
articles.abstract: Personalized, generative AI systems increasingly adapt their behavior to individual users over time, fundamentally changing model behavior. While existing auditing approaches have been effective at surfacing harms in non-personalized contexts, they often rely on static, simulated evaluations and definitions of harm that aggregate across broad, group categories. In this position paper, we argue that such approaches can fail to capture emergent harms in personalized generative AI systems, where harms surface through interpretations of ongoing interaction and evolve with user history. We identify three presuppositions underlying many harm auditing paradigms: that harms can be (1) specified outside real-world interaction, (2) defined non-pluralistically within groups, and (3) treated as static. One might argue that personalized systems could simply learn definitions of what constitutes harm to individual users through repeated interactions. However, we argue that attempts to surface user harms through deeper personalization risk imposing asymmetric burdens of labor and privacy on marginalized users. Consequently, we propose reframing understandings of harm as adaptive, user- and community-centered processes, and outline design directions that shift auditing from retrospective evaluation toward infrastructures that support ongoing articulation of harm in interaction. Our work highlights the need for auditing and design practices that better reflect the pluralistic and evolving nature of harm understanding in personalized generative AI systems.

articles.title: Autonomous AI research agents in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma immunology: from multimodal evidence to experimental validation
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational–experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.

articles.title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate--Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents
articles.abstract: Large language models, and the agents built on them, spend an ever-growing share of their compute and memory on remembering: caching attention keys and values, carrying long prompts, maintaining recurrent state, and storing what happened in previous turns and sessions. Because none of this memory is free, four largely separate research communities have each learned to compact it. They evict or quantize the KV cache, prune or distill prompts, bound architectural state, and consolidate agent memory. We argue that these are instances of one problem: a rate--distortion decision about what context-derived information to retain versus discard, at what fidelity, under a resource budget, so as to preserve downstream task utility. We make this lens precise with a single compaction objective and a layer-agnostic lower bound, use it to build a seven-axis taxonomy that classifies methods from across the stack uniformly, and use it to transfer mechanisms between layers that have never been connected, from serving-stack KV management to agent long-term memory. Two patterns hold across the survey. At every layer the signal that decides what to keep is attention magnitude or recency, and it fails in the same way everywhere, by discarding, before the query is known and with no way to undo it, information the query later needs. And while compression is measured carefully on single-turn long context, the repeated compaction that agents actually perform is almost never measured, and no benchmark holds one budget axis across all the layers at once. We turn both observations into a benchmark proposal, a small reference experiment, and a set of compaction-aware design principles, and we map the open problems.

articles.title: A Multi-Agent AI Optimization System for Improving Rig Utilization and Production Gains in the Burgan Field
articles.abstract: Abstract Scheduling a fleet of workover rigs across a mature giant field requires balancing production objectives against a dense web of operational constraints: artificial lift readiness, material availability, location doability, site and pad access, and rig–well compatibility. In the Greater Burgan complex, this forward planning has historically been built and maintained manually in the well delivery management (WDM) system, an in-house rig-scheduling application in which of the order of ten stakeholder teams continuously record and revise workover activities and their constraints. Across a typical year, the programme spans on the order of 500 workover wells and roughly 40 active rigs; distributing that fleet across the candidate wells and their ordered sequences yields a combinatorial space of astronomical size, on the order of hundreds of septillions of feasible arrangements and beyond, that cannot be searched by hand. This paper describes the design, deployment, and field evaluation of a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) scheduling system introduced by the Operator's Integration Excellence team to optimize the 90-day forward plan across the full workover operation of approximately 40 rigs and 200 workover wells. The system decomposes scheduling across cooperating agents: data preprocessing, rig–well resource matching, constraint validation, schedule optimization by a genetic algorithm adapted to the Operator's scheduling rules and operating over short- and long-term memory, execution monitoring, and feedback, with a human-in-the-loop review and approval workflow retained throughout. Planners select one of two objective modes (maximize production gain or meet a specified production target) while the optimizer enforces stability rules that protect active and next-scheduled jobs, group multi-well sites, and honor rig–well compatibility. Performance was evaluated by comparing manually prepared schedules against system-optimized schedules over identical planning inputs and, separately, through historical validation (backtesting) over rolling 90-day look-back windows. To respect data-confidentiality requirements, production results are reported in normalized form and absolute volumes are withheld. In a field-wide evaluation, the optimized schedule increased the projected 90-day production gain by 16% over the manual baseline, an advantage that compounded across the horizon, while fleet-average rig idle time fell by 46% and schedule preparation collapsed from about ten days of manual coordination to minutes of computation. The paper presents the constraint taxonomy and scheduling logic in transferable form and outlines an ongoing extension to new-drill planning, where injector–producer relationships, injection timing, and rig-contract capability introduce additional considerations.

articles.title: Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching for Large Language Models
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-term interaction, task continuity, experience reuse, and collaborative problem-solving. However, existing memory architectures often emphasize individual memory management, shared memory repositories, or predefined collaboration strategies. These approaches leave an important design question: how can multiple memory perspectives generated by the same model coexist with memories maintained by heterogeneous models, while the system adaptively determines when to operate independently and when to exchange information? This paper proposes Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching (PW-ASMS), a unified framework that combines parallel memory worlds, adaptive self-memory, shared-memory collaboration, and cross-model memory integration. Parallel memory worlds are created by assigning different memory orientations to instances of the same underlying model. Each world independently selects, organizes, updates, and retrieves experiences according to its designated orientation. A dynamic controller subsequently determines whether an agent should rely on its own memory, exchange information with other parallel worlds, consult a shared memory repository, or combine these operations. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs whose memories can contribute complementary information to a common collaborative process. The proposed architecture consists of parallel memory worlds, individual memory stores, a governed shared memory layer, a memory evaluation module, and an adaptive switching controller. A utility-based decision mechanism considers task relevance, information novelty, confidence, memory consistency, communication cost, privacy constraints, and expected downstream benefit. The framework is designed to reduce unnecessary information exchange while preserving opportunities for collaborative knowledge acquisition. We formulate research questions, operational procedures, evaluation metrics, and experimental comparisons to assess its effectiveness. The paper provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for investigating adaptive memory organization in multi-agent LLM systems; its effectiveness remains to be established empirically.

articles.title: In-Parameter Learning: Why Lifelong AI Systems Need More Than Longer Context
articles.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to interact with changing users, tools, and environments over extended periods of time. However, current systems remain largely static: their parameters are fixed during deployment, while new experiences, domain knowledge, corrections, and behavioral adaptations are handled primarily through external memory management and in-context learning. In this position paper, we focus on lifelong AI: AI systems that can continually learn from their long-term experience throughout an extended deployment lifetime. This position paper argues that existing in-context mechanisms are insufficient for lifelong AI, and advocate In-Parameter Learning (IPL) as a necessary complement to In-Context Learning (ICL), referring to mechanisms that allow a deployed model to continually and safely update its parameters during use. More broadly, we aim to renew the community’s attention to in-parameter learning and to recalibrate the overly optimistic expectations placed on in-context learning alone. Our central claim is that future lifelong AI systems should be built around a hybrid paradigm: in-context learning for immediate, provisional, and reversible information, and in-parameter learning for durable, cumulative, and generalizable growth.

articles.title: Adaptive Switching between Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration for Multiple Large Language Models
articles.abstract: Multiple large language models (LLMs) can explore complex problem spaces independently or collaboratively. Autonomous exploration allows each model to develop distinct hypotheses, investigate alternative solution paths, and reduce premature convergence caused by shared assumptions. Collaborative exploration enables models to exchange findings, identify complementary information, resolve disagreements, and construct solutions using distributed knowledge. However, consistently relying on either exploration mode may limit problem-solving effectiveness. Permanent autonomous exploration can produce redundant investigations and prevent useful knowledge exchange, whereas permanent collaborative exploration can encourage premature consensus, correlated errors, and the suppression of unconventional ideas. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration for Multiple Large Language Models (ASACE), a framework in which multiple LLM agents dynamically switch between independent exploration and collaborative exploration according to the evolving characteristics of the task. Rather than prescribing a fixed collaboration schedule, ASACE evaluates exploration progress, estimated information gain, inter-agent disagreement, search redundancy, solution quality, and computational cost to determine the appropriate exploration mode at each decision point. The framework incorporates autonomous exploration, selective knowledge exchange, collaborative exploration, outcome evaluation, and adaptive mode selection into a unified iterative process. A mode-selection mechanism is formulated to balance exploration diversity, collective learning, solution quality, and resource efficiency. The framework also introduces an optional hysteresis mechanism to reduce unstable switching between exploration modes. This paper formalizes the proposed framework, presents its algorithmic procedure, discusses implementation strategies, and develops an experimental protocol for evaluating its effectiveness. Comparisons with permanently autonomous, permanently collaborative, and fixed-schedule hybrid baselines are proposed across reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, software engineering, scientific discovery, and search tasks. The central hypothesis is that adaptive switching can improve the balance between independent discovery and collective knowledge utilization when task conditions vary over time. The paper provides a research framework and testable hypotheses rather than claiming experimentally established improvements. Its contribution is the explicit formulation of exploration-mode selection as a dynamic control problem for multi-LLM systems.

articles.title: From plausible menus to trustworthy nutrition: a risk-proportionate VALID-Diet framework for artificial intelligence-generated dietary advice
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can produce menus, recipes, shopping lists, and dietary explanations that appear individualized and clinically informed. Fluency alone, however, provides little evidence of nutritional accuracy, safety, feasibility, or benefit. We propose VALID-Diet, a staged framework for evaluating systems that generate actionable dietary recommendations as sociotechnical interventions. Its domains are Verification of nutritional targets and composition; Adversarial safety and boundary testing; Linkage between user inputs and recommendation changes; Implementation feasibility and inclusion; and Documentation, versioning, and reproducibility. Stage 0 defines intended use, input integrity, and a structured risk profile based on harm severity, exposure, autonomy, reversibility, and enforceable oversight. Stage 1 separates target validity, menu achievement, and arithmetic agreement and, for integrated systems, tests retrieval, calculation, and generation as distinct components. Stage 2 evaluates safety, substantive personalization, feasibility, and inclusion using pre-specified case blueprints. Stage 3 evaluates human oversight, workflow utility, and prospective outcomes only after earlier gates are passed. A retrospective worked application to a published retrieval-augmented personalized-nutrition system illustrates risk assignment and progression decisions. VALID-Diet is not a regulatory standard or consensus guideline; it is a testable proposal intended to align research claims with evidentiary strength.

articles.title: Multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis in the post-BPaLM era: from genomic resistance prediction to precision treatment, therapeutic failure and transmission control — a comprehensive review
articles.abstract: Abstract Background Multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) remains a leading cause of death from antimicrobial resistance. The six-month, all-oral regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) has transformed care. It is shorter, safer and more effective than earlier regimens. Yet its long-term success is fragile. Resistance to the newest drugs is already emerging, and access to fast, accurate resistance testing is uneven. Objective This review examines how genomic resistance prediction, precision treatment, the management of therapeutic failure and transmission control can be joined into a single, practical framework for the post-BPaLM era. Methods We conducted a comprehensive narrative review. We searched five databases and hand-searched key references, WHO guidance and pivotal trials. We then purposively synthesized 47 authenticated sources. They spanned randomized trials, genomic and bioinformatic studies, molecular epidemiology, mechanistic work and World Health Organization (WHO) guidance. Results BPaLM achieves favorable outcomes in about 89% of patients, against roughly half with older regimens. Whole-genome and targeted sequencing can predict resistance for much of the drug panel, although genotype–phenotype concordance is still incomplete for several newer drugs. Bedaquiline resistance, driven mainly by Rv0678 variants, and its cross-resistance with clofazimine are the most pressing threats. Linezolid toxicity still limits treatment and calls for dose personalization and monitoring. Genomic surveillance can detect transmission clusters early and feed data back into stewardship. Machine learning adds value, with the strongest current evidence in resistance prediction. Conclusion We propose a closed loop for the post-BPaLM era. Rapid sequencing should guide personalized regimens. Toxicity and resistance should be watched in real time. Genomic surveillance should protect the new drugs at the population level. Equity of access must underpin all of it.

articles.title: Applications of Generative AI for Advancing Scientific Content Production, Evaluation and Dissemination
articles.abstract: Generative AI is becoming part of how scientific content is being produced, evaluated and communicated. Large language models (LLMs) can write science news, simulate readers, retrieve evidence, generate scientific hypotheses, write code, and execute research workflows. These capabilities create opportunities for accelerating scientific discovery and broadening access to scientific information, but they also introduce risks related to hallucination and trustworthiness. This doctoral dissertation studies how generative AI can support scientific content production and dissemination, while preserving trust, comprehension, and replicability. The completed work includes three components: (1) detecting LLM-generated science news through SANews and GFS, (2) evaluating science communication through reader learning using KnowledgeGain and LLMSim, and (3) benchmarking LLM agents for research replication with ReplicatorBench and ReplicatorAgent. The proposed work extends these directions toward learning-optimized science news generation, MESH for multimodal evidence-grounded hypothesis generation, and MERIT, a simulation-grounded framework for evaluating autonomous AI co-scientists and hypothesis testing in computational materials discovery. The overarching goal is to develop evaluation methods and AI systems that make scientific outputs not only fluent and scalable, but also grounded, useful, and interpretable.

articles.title: Digital Twins as Socio-Technical Decision Systems: A Comparative Systematic Review of Supply Chain Management and Healthcare
articles.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is rapidly evolving from a digital representation of physical assets into a decision-support infrastructure that integrates real-time data, analytics, and simulation. However, existing research remains fragmented across application domains, limiting understanding of how DTs enable decision-making under different socio-technical conditions. This study presents a systematic literature review and decision-centric comparative analysis of DT applications in two contrasting decision environments: Supply Chain Management (SCM) and healthcare. Following a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) protocol, 193 peer-reviewed studies (95 SCM and 98 healthcare) were identified, screened, and synthesized across six analytical dimensions: application domains, technological integration, decision-making levels, business value, stakeholder involvement, and implementation challenges. The findings reveal fundamentally different decision logics despite a shared technological foundation based on Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud computing. SCM-DTs primarily support coordination, optimization, resilience, and organizational scalability, whereas healthcare-DTs emphasize personalization, patient safety, and ethical governance under stringent regulatory constraints. Building on these findings, the study proposes a decision-centric comparative framework and a value–complexity perspective suggesting that value realization is increasingly associated with technological, organizational, and governance complexity as DT ecosystems mature. The paper advances the conceptualization of DTs as socio-technical decision systems and provides practical guidance for researchers, managers, and policymakers seeking responsible and effective digital transformation.

articles.title: Solving Specification Drift and Contextual Degradation via a Tri-Stream Cognitive Architecture with Non-Lossy Canonical Synthesis in Autonomous AI Agents
articles.abstract: Long-running conversational AI agents and assistive development models inevitably succumb to contextual degradation, specification drift, and sycophantic decay. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms treat dialogue turns, human identity, and technical parameters as an undifferentiated, flat vector repository. This structural limitation induces lossy compression of technical truth, context window pollution, and hallucinatory synthesis of project constraints. This paper introduces the architecture of Blue Synergy CORTEX, an external, persistent cognitive runtime operating via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and stateful REST gateways. CORTEX establishes an architectural Tri-Stream Memory Boundary, bifurcating context into three distinct operational lifecycles: an evolving User Stream (Cognitive Blueprint), an audited Identity Stream (Executive Calibration with immutable Core Axioms), and an invariant, non-decaying Knowledge Stream (Living Canonical Specifications). To permanently eliminate specification drift, the Knowledge Stream utilizes a Dual-Zone Ingestion Pattern that couples sub-20ms fast-append staging buffers with scheduled, non-destructive canonical refactoring governed by an algorithmic Semantic Invariant Guard. Operational telemetry is protected by a Cognitive Immunity Shield, ensuring runtime tool crashes and apologetic model artifacts are filtered from long-term memory. Context retrieval executes via a deterministic, zero-LLM topological pathway achieving sub-65ms latency. Finally, we formalize the compliance model under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, Articles 5, 14, and 15), backed by quantitative benchmark metrics demonstrating 98% factual faithfulness and a 2% hallucination rate.

articles.title: Auditing Alignment Controllability in LLMs via Political Axes
articles.abstract: Political audits of large language models (LLMs) usually reduce each to one point on a political compass. But that resting point barely matters in deployment: a model must land somewhere, and what counts is how far, and in which directions, its answers can be steered. That steering runs through the system prompt: the personalization layer a platform sets, or one induced from a user's history, not necessarily written by hand. We run a dispersion-first stress test of prompt-based controllability across 12 ideological personas plus an unsteered baseline, 70 Political Compass items, ten replicates, and seven leading LLMs: GPT-5, Claude, Grok, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, and Qwen (63,700 responses). Contextual framing explains roughly 88%-93% of variance on the economic and society axes, model identity under 3%: responses are highly instruction-adjustable. Models do not shift alike: some move more, and some saturate under extreme framings. Conflicting directional-steering results in prior audits resolve once baselines are recognized as non-centered: displacement and proximity diverge, so the effect is geometric, not differential compliance. Under authoritarian prompts, models produce similar shifts on the same questions. Political-coordinate audits therefore need steerability audits reporting dispersion, symmetry, saturation, and refusal floors. We release prompts, benchmark data, and code.

articles.title: FHIR-AgentEval: a modular sandbox for benchmarking clinical LLM agents with memory-augmented configurations
articles.abstract: Healthcare data exchange increasingly relies on HL7 FHIR, but FHIR’s implementation complexity creates barriers for clinical workflows. Large language model (LLM) agents could bridge this gap by translating natural language requests into structured FHIR operations, yet their reliability remains unproven. We present FHIR-AgentEval, an extensible evaluation sandbox comprising 43 modular tasks for benchmarking LLM agents on realistic appointment management and genetic testing workflows. Each task executes against a resettable FHIR server with custom deterministic validation of both agent responses and resulting server state. We run an ablation study of five agent configurations, varying access to an on-demand FHIR R4 specifications server and long-term memory trained with or without specification grounding. Across four experimental settings, memory consistently improves task success and reduces strategic failures such as incorrect tool selection and resource-type confusion. On held-out tasks, the best memory configuration improves success by 9.1% over baseline, offering a potential pathway toward more robust clinical deployment.

articles.title: Evaluation of physical training effectiveness for college students based on deep reinforcement learning
articles.abstract: The physical training of college students can be made more productive with the help of adaptive approaches. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offers training policies that are more customized based on performance and physiological measurements and are superior to fixed schedules. The first goal is to make a smart system that will be efficient in physical training optimization with the help of DRL. Research suggests the Hare Escape-Search Functional Dueling Deep Q-Network (HE-FDDQN), which is a DRL algorithm that predicts student states, actions, and rewards in order to maximize training policies. Dueling architecture improves state-value learning, while escape-search enhances exploration for adaptive offline training recommendations. The College Student Physical Training Dataset was used for evaluation, which is a public data set consisting of 1000 records from the measurements of the wearable devices, fitness tests, and self-reported physical activity indicators. Preprocessing includes data cleaning, synchronization of data, and normalization of data. Python implementations exhibit effective policy learning, and visualization reveals that the development of fitness and less overtraining is possible. The HE-FDDQN model demonstrated great regression ability (MAE 1.17, RMSE 1.52, R 2 0.931), and good classification scores, recall 0.922, precision 0.913, accuracy 0.925, AUC 0.912, and F1-score 0.909. The Dueling DQN strategy achieved better rewards and convergence, supporting adaptive recommendations under offline experimental evaluation. Overall, the results suggest that HE-FDDQN can enhance the assessment and personalization of college students' physical training, offering an efficient and customized alternative to fixed training plans with the potential to improve fitness outcomes.

articles.title: AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding
articles.abstract: Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent's long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

articles.title: MemPoison: Bypassing Selective Memory Mechanisms to Plant Backdoors in LLM Agents
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly leverage long-term memory to support persistent and autonomous task execution. However, this capability also introduces a new attack surface: memory poisoning, where adversaries can inject malicious information to influence future behavior. Existing memory poisoning attacks often assume that injected content can be stored directly in memory, overlooking the selective extraction and rewriting stages in modern memory pipelines. This makes prior methods ineffective under realistic settings. In this paper, we propose MemPoison, a novel memory poisoning attack that bypasses selective memory mechanisms in LLM agents, where an attacker can inject triggerable backdoors into the agent's long-term memory through dialogue interactions, thereby misleading its subsequent responses. MemPoison introduces three key components: (i) a semantic relational bridge that binds the trigger and payload into a coherent statement to ensure their co-extraction into memory; (ii) entity masquerading that optimizes triggers to mimic named entities, resisting rewriting; and (iii) joint embedding optimization that shapes trigger-injected texts into a tight cluster in the embedding space while maintaining isolation from benign embeddings for stealth. Evaluations across different agent domains and memory mechanisms show MemPoison achieves attack success rates up to 0.95, outperforming existing baselines. Mechanistic analysis reveals the exploitation of embedding-space anisotropy and attention redistribution, highlighting core vulnerabilities in selective memory systems. We evaluate multiple defense strategies and demonstrate their fundamental limitations in mitigating the attack. We release our code to facilitate further research.

articles.title: MemMorph: Tool Hijacking in LLM Agents via Memory Poisoning
articles.abstract: LLM-driven agents are capable of selecting external tools to complete users' tasks. However, attackers could compromise such process, steering agents toward inappropriate/wrong tools and enabling malicious actions. Most existing attacks primarily manipulate the tool metadata, which is easily detectable by auditing and may lose effectiveness as modern agents increasingly adopt memory modules to refine tool selection policies through accumulated experience. This paper proposes MemMorph, the first attack that bias tool selection by poisoning the agent's long-term memory. Rather than explicitly dictating the tool invocation decision, MemMorph injects a small number of crafted records that are disguised as technical facts, incident reports, and operational policies. These poisoned records reshape the agent's contextual perception and decision-making process, leading it to autonomously infer and select the tool preferred by the attacker. Experiments across 3 benchmarks, 10 agent backbones, and 3 memory-module implementations show that MemMorph achieves up to 85.9% attack success rate with only three injected records, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 25% while retaining potency under 3 representative defenses. Our findings expose long-term memory as a critical and under-explored attack surface in tool-augmented agents, urging the development of memory-level integrity safeguards.

articles.title: Trojan Hippo Bench: A Dynamic Benchmark for Persistent Memory Attacks and Defenses in LLM Agents
articles.abstract: Memory systems enable otherwise stateless LLM agents to persist user information across sessions, but also introduce a new attack surface. The Trojan Hippo attack is a class of persistent memory attacks that operates under a more realistic threat model than prior memory poisoning work. The attacker plants a dormant payload into an agent's long-term memory via a single untrusted tool call (e.g., a crafted email), which activates only when the user later discusses sensitive topics such as finance, health, or identity, and exfiltrates high-value personal data to the attacker. While anecdotal demonstrations of such attacks have appeared against deployed systems, no prior work systematically evaluates them across heterogeneous memory architectures and defenses. We introduce Trojan Hippo Bench, a dynamic evaluation framework for persistent memory attacks and memory-layer defenses, comprising two components, (1) an OpenEvolve-based adaptive red-teaming benchmark that stress-tests defenses and memory backends against continuously refined attacks, and (2) a capability-aware security-utility analysis for persistent memory systems, enabling principled reasoning about defense deployment across different usage profiles. Instantiated on an email assistant across four memory backends (explicit tool memory, agentic memory, RAG, and sliding-window context), the undefended Trojan Hippo attack achieves up to 85-100% attack success rate (ASR) against current frontier models from OpenAI and Google, with planted memories successfully activating even after 100 benign sessions. We evaluate four memory-system defenses inspired by basic security principles; they reduce attack success to as low as 0-5%, but at utility costs that vary widely with the task mix. Effective real-world deployment thus remains an open challenge that Trojan Hippo Bench is built to study; we release it to support reuse and extension.

articles.title: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval
articles.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to persist experiences and refine future performance. While this experience learning capability enhances agentic autonomy, it introduces a critical, unexplored attack surface, i.e., the trust boundary between an agent's reasoning core and its own past. In this paper, we introduce MemoryGraft. It is a novel indirect injection attack that compromises agent behavior not through immediate jailbreaks, but by implanting malicious successful experiences into the agent's long-term memory. Unlike traditional prompt injections that are transient, or standard RAG poisoning that targets factual knowledge, MemoryGraft exploits the agent's semantic imitation heuristic which is the tendency to replicate patterns from retrieved successful tasks. We demonstrate that an attacker who can supply benign ingestion-level artifacts that the agent reads during execution can induce it to construct a poisoned RAG store where a small set of malicious procedure templates is persisted alongside benign experiences. When the agent later encounters semantically similar tasks, union retrieval over lexical and embedding similarity reliably surfaces these grafted memories, and the agent adopts the embedded unsafe patterns, leading to persistent behavioral drift across sessions. We validate MemoryGraft on MetaGPT's DataInterpreter agent with GPT-4o and find that a small number of poisoned records can account for a large fraction of retrieved experiences on benign workloads, turning experience-based self-improvement into a vector for stealthy and durable compromise. To facilitate reproducibility and future research, our code and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/Jacobhhy/Agent-Memory-Poisoning.
